title: Choose, then trust
hook: think long before making a friend, then trust them wholly

segments.voice: Yesterday: who is poor, the one who craves more. Your line was crave less. Did one want shrink a size? Day four hundred thirty-five.

Lucilius has sent Seneca some letters, carried by a man he calls his friend. And in the very same note, he adds: but please don't discuss my affairs with him. You can almost hear Seneca put the letter down and raise an eyebrow. A friend you can't talk in front of? It's a small slip, the kind any of us make. We call someone a friend after two good dinners, and then we're careful around them for years. Seneca's third letter takes that slip and turns it inside out. Today: choose, then trust.
screen: `MY FRIEND. BUT DON'T TELL HIM.` → `A RAISED EYEBROW.` → `CHOOSE, THEN TRUST.`

segments.voice: First, the word friend. Seneca says Lucilius is using it loosely, the way people greet anyone as dear sir. Either this man is a real friend, or he isn't. If he is, trust him. If he isn't, don't call him one. Second, the order. Then the rule. Think for a long time about whether someone should be admitted to your friendship. But once you've decided, welcome them with your whole heart, and speak as boldly with them as with yourself. Judge before the friendship. Trust after it. Seneca says some people get this backwards, citing the philosopher Theophrastus: they love first and judge later, and then they can't decide whether to keep loving. Third, the two mistakes. Some people tell everything to anyone who will listen, he says, unloading secrets into any ear they meet. Others won't confide even in those closest to them, and lock away every thought. Both are faults. One trusts everyone. The other trusts no one. Fourth, why it matters. The care in choosing is what makes the trust possible. If you take a long time over the gate, you don't have to stand guard inside the house. That doesn't mean a friend can never let you down. Seneca knew betrayal well; he lived at Nero's court. It means that once you've chosen, you stop treating your friend like a suspect. Friendship, for Seneca, is one of the few things outside us that's worth giving ourselves to completely. But only after we've looked carefully at who we're giving ourselves to.
screen: `A FRIEND, OR NOT A FRIEND.` · `JUDGE FIRST, THEN TRUST WHOLLY.` · `TRUSTING ALL, TRUSTING NONE.` · `CARE AT THE GATE, PEACE INSIDE.` · then, large: `CHOOSE, THEN TRUST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've already chosen, someone who has shown you over time who they are. See their face. Now notice if there's anything you've been holding back from them out of habit, not because of anything they did. A worry, a hope, a thank you. You don't have to say it now. Just picture telling them plainly, the way you'd say it to yourself. Notice how that feels in your chest. Breathe with the trust, not the guard. The bell holds the time.
Choose. Seneca's third letter: think long before you call someone a friend; once you have, trust them as you trust yourself. Today's word.
Your line: choose, then trust. Today, tell one chosen friend one true thing you've been keeping back for no good reason. Day four hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Following Seneca, some people are slow and careful about whom they call a close friend, and then speak openly with those they've chosen.

original.script: post amicitiam credendum est, ante amicitiam iudicandum
original.say: post a-MI-ki-tee-am kre-DEN-dum est, AN-teh a-MI-ki-tee-am yoo-di-KAN-dum
original.note: Latin: after friendship, trust; before friendship, judge. From Seneca's third letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: be careful who you trust.
what it means: Seneca says be careful who you choose, and then trust them completely; the care comes first so the trust can be whole.
what a scholar hears: Seneca frames it against Theophrastus, Aristotle's successor, which shows the Stoic letters freely using other schools.

notes: Letter 3.1: Lucilius sent letters by a 'friend' but asked Seneca not to discuss his affairs with him; 3.2: 'post amicitiam credendum est, ante amicitiam iudicandum' and the reference to Theophrastus; 3.4: those who tell everyone everything and those who confide in no one, both faults. Paraphrased; confirm.
The Theophrastus attribution (those who judge after they have loved, contrary to his precepts): confirm reading of Letter 3.2.
'Seneca knew betrayal well; he lived at Nero's court' is an interpretive aside; confirm tone.
